narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year performance in law school had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the 4th decile is noticeably below the average of 6th decile among students who were accepted, signaling that your early grades were weaker than most successful applicants. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure; your score of 35 sits below the 37.2 average of admitted students. These two elements together created a clear picture of elevated risk.

Your third-year performance worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the chance of failure. Ranking in the 5th decile placed you close to the 5.8 average of accepted students, showing meaningful improvement over time.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role in this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Demonstrating consistent high performance in later law school years can help offset earlier weaknesses. Many students successfully reapply after targeted improvement in these key areas. (218 words)
